title: FLOD System: First Line Of Defense
subtitle: An adaptive two stage Layer 4 volumetric DDoS mitigation gateway

stages.title: Stage 1: Packet capture
stages.description: A Rust sensor sits on the packet path and sees every packet bound for a protected host. Two interchangeable backends fill the same per window counters.
steps: A packet arrives on the ingress interface of the gateway.
The libpcap backend reads it through a BPF filter that drops everything not addressed to a protected host.
The kernel backend does the same in XDP (driver mode where the NIC supports it) with a TC program on egress, counting into per CPU maps.
Egress packets only increment a counter, so past mitigation never shapes future decisions.

stages.title: Stage 1: Windows and features
stages.description: Traffic is condensed into one summary per window, so nothing downstream needs to look at individual packets.
steps: A window closes on a packet count, elapsed time, or a timer tick.
Source entropy measures how spread out the sending addresses are. A flood from one address has low entropy.
A smoothed packet rate measures volume.
Source port entropy, TTL variance and TCP SYN fingerprint diversity add features that address spoofing cannot forge.
Their histograms are keyed by value, not by source, so a flood of random addresses cannot fill them.

stages.title: Stage 1: Adaptive baseline
stages.description: Each protected host learns its own normal. The anomaly boundary moves with the traffic instead of using one fixed threshold.
steps: A warm-up period of 200 windows builds the first baseline for a host.
Welford accumulators keep a running mean and standard deviation of rate and entropy.
A window is flagged when the rate exceeds mean plus k sigma, or entropy falls below mean minus k sigma.
Flagged windows do not update the baseline, which defends against an attacker ramping slowly to poison it.
A bounded freeze lets the baseline accept sustained legitimate growth.
Sigma floors are calibrated from measured Normal traffic and set through an environment file.

stages.title: The handoff between stages
stages.description: Stage 1 sends a fixed size feature vector per window to Stage 2 over a Unix domain socket.
steps: Stage 1 reports flagged windows and a heartbeat for quiet hosts.
Each vector is 216 bytes with a fixed field order, including a warm-up flag.
Stage 2 verifies the peer on the socket is root or the sensor's account before reading.
Stage 2 never waits on a lock or a subprocess in its receive loop, so the socket does not back up.

stages.title: Stage 2: Classification
stages.description: A Random Forest decides what kind of traffic a flagged window is. An Isolation Forest flags traffic unlike anything in training.
steps: The Random Forest labels the window Normal, Flash Crowd or DDoS.
Telling a flash crowd from an attack is the one thing a fixed threshold cannot do.
The Isolation Forest scores how unusual the window is and can surface it as Anomalous for review, without changing enforcement.
Deterministic safety overrides catch extreme spikes whatever the models say, including during warm-up.
Both models skip warm-up windows, whose statistics have not settled.

stages.title: Stage 2: Enforcement
stages.description: Four tiers act on attacks, escalating from reversible throttling to blocking only where the source is confidently identified.
steps: Tier 1 blocks the dominant source when it is concentrated and fast.
Tier 2 blocks any single source far above human rates, however the attack is spread.
Tier 3 rate limits sources that are elevated but ambiguous.
Tier 4 throttles every active flow to the host when traffic is spread too thin to name a source.
Blocks need consecutive attack windows, so one noisy window cannot trigger one.
Rules live in ipsets with an expiry, so a wrong decision heals itself. A whitelist protects known good addresses.

stages.title: Dashboard, alerts and reports
stages.description: Operators see every host's state, act on addresses by hand, and get notified and documented without leaving the gateway.
steps: The dashboard is served by Stage 2 over HTTPS on port 8000, with logins and account management.
Pages cover targets, active flows, logs, interfaces, firewall state, alerts and playbooks.
Alerts go out through Discord or SMTP, with credentials redacted from any failure message.
Playbooks run timed sequences on a trigger, such as escalating a target or generating a report.
Incident reports are rendered on the server from the database as PDF.

stages.title: The learning loop
stages.description: The system captures what it saw, and a person decides what it learns from. Nothing retrains itself on an unverified guess.
steps: Windows the models doubted or called DDoS are staged in capture files.
Automatic labeling labels a staged row only when two independently trained models agree with enough confidence.
The Auto Label page shows the staged rows for review and merging, an operator's deliberate click.
A trim tool caps the DDoS class at the size of the other two, dropping whole sessions.
Models are retrained with leave one session out validation, which picks the tree depth.

stages.title: Benchmarking the gateway
stages.description: A live benchmark drives the lab's generators through seven traffic phases per capture backend and reports what the deployed system did.
steps: Normal, Flash Crowd and attack traffic run alone, then in every pairing, then all three.
Each backend learns its own baseline, and enforcement is reset before every run.
The report covers detection, enforcement, CPU, memory, drops and Stage 2 latency.
A probe measures packet latency through the gateway, with jitter and loss, in every phase.
A limit ladder raises the packet rate step by step, with small and large packets, to find the peak and loss-free packets per second and Mbit/s.
All results come from the simulated lab environment.
